headline: Bunker Pinned Tight From Mattituck to Plum Gut, and the Bass Finally Noticed
subhead: The new moon squeezed bait against every rock on the North Fork this week — here's where it's paying off and where it isn't yet.
body_markdown:
Sixty years back my father used to say you could smell the bunker before you saw them — that oily, iron smell that comes off a pod of a few thousand fish getting nervous all at once. I remember standing on the bluff at Horton Point with him one September, watching a raft of bunker pushed up so tight against the rocks the water looked black, and something big working underneath it like a plow turning sod. He didn't say a word. Just handed me the rod and pointed. That's the North Fork in September, same as it's always been, and this past week it happened again, right on schedule.

The new moon on the 10th put the strongest tidal push of the early fall through the Sound, and it did exactly what a strong push does this time of year — it squeezed the bunker schools tight against the beaches, the inlets, and the river mouths from Mattituck clear through to Orient. Water's still carrying some late-summer warmth on the west end — Kings Point over on the other shore was reading close to 71 degrees — but out here on the east end, off Orient and toward the Gut, it's running cooler, closer to 69. That gradient matters. The cooler water at the east end is where the bait's been getting nervous first, and where the bass have been leaning into it hardest.

We said last week that the bunker schools tightening up from Raritan Bay through the Sound would get the stripers past the stragglers-and-pickers stage and into real commitment, and that's what's showing up now. This isn't scattered activity anymore — boats working bunker schools off Rocky Point and out past Orient are seeing bass actually committing to the bait, not just tailing it. That's the difference between a fish that swats at a plug out of habit and one that's actually feeding.

Best producer this week has been the simplest one — snag a bunker off the top of a tight school with a treble, drop it back on a fish-finder rig, and let it sit on bottom in 15 to 25 feet along the Rocky Point and Horton Point rock edges. Guys working bucktails behind the bunker pods, 2 to 3 ounce white or bunker-colored, have done well too on the drift, especially working the seam where the school breaks off the rocks into deeper water on the last of the ebb. Sizes have been mixed — slot fish mostly, a few over, nothing to write home about yet in terms of numbers, but the fish are there and they're eating with intent, which after a slow August counts for something.

Snapper blues are thick in every back creek and marina basin from Mattituck to Orient, which if you've fished this shore as long as I have, you know is the tell. Adult blues follow that snapper show by a few weeks most years, and there's word of bigger blues starting to filter in behind the bunker schools at the inlets — nothing sustained yet, more like fish showing up in the same water as the bass and taking their share when the school gets pinned. If you're throwing metal at a bass blitz this week, don't be surprised if something with better teeth grabs it first.

Porgy fishing keeps doing what it does every September — quietly improving. The rock piles off Horton Point and the structure out toward Orient are holding good numbers now that the water's easing off its summer peak. Sandworms and clam on a simple hi-lo rig, right on the bottom, still the way to go. Nothing flashy about it, but it's about as reliable a bite as this shore offers right now, and it's a good option on a day when the bass aren't cooperating.

Fluke is the one I'd steer you away from for now. The better fish have already staged off toward deeper, cooler water ahead of their fall exit — that's a pattern that happens every year about this time, and this year's no different. What's left inshore along our beaches is mostly short fish. If fluke's the target, you're better off putting your time into porgy or bass right now and letting the fluke go do what they do.

Weakfish have been mixed in here and there with the bass on bunker chunks near the river mouths — Mattituck Creek mouth, the mouth at Rocky Point — but it's not a directed bite, more a fish or two showing up in the box as a bonus. Wouldn't plan a trip around it.

Looking ahead, the tidal push from this new moon should hold its strength for another few days before it starts easing off, and that's the window to work with. The bunker aren't going anywhere fast with this much current pinning them to structure, and the bass have shown they're willing to commit to it. If you've only got one day this week, fish the last two hours of the ebb at Rocky Point or out toward Orient, right where the bait gets squeezed against the rocks — that's been the pattern all week and there's no reason to think it changes before the tides ease back. Toward Plum Gut, the current's been ripping hard enough on the new-moon tides to make boat control the real challenge more than finding fish — respect that water, it doesn't forgive a bad drift. Keep an eye on wind out of the northeast, which would push more bait and cooler water down the Sound and could tighten this pattern up even further by the weekend.
